def: Identity and Access Management: the part of AWS that decides, for every request, whether the caller is allowed to do it.
The login an AWS account was created with. It can do everything and no IAM policy can limit it, so it gets MFA and is almost never used.
An identity with no password and no permanent keys. Whatever assumes it gets temporary credentials that expire on their own.
A JSON document of statements, each with an Effect, Actions and Resources, that allows or denies requests.
Giving each identity exactly the actions and resources it needs, and nothing more.
A long-lived ID and secret that let a program call AWS. It works until deleted, so a leaked one is dangerous. Prefer roles.
The part of a role that says who or what may assume it, such as the EC2 service.
A policy statement with Effect Deny that matches a request. It beats every Allow.
The default answer in IAM: if no policy allows a request, it is denied.
Amazon Resource Name: the unique ID of an AWS resource, like arn:aws:s3:::quickcart-menu-photos-111122223333.
The Domain Name System: turns a name like example.com into an IP address, through a chain of servers.
Where a domain's DNS records live in Route 53. It only takes effect once the registrar points to its name servers.
The servers in charge of a domain's records. The registrar tells the world which ones they are.
The company you bought a domain from. It sets which name servers answer for the domain.
A Route 53 record that points a name, even the domain's root, at an AWS resource such as a load balancer, and follows its addresses as they change.
Time to live: how many seconds a DNS answer may be cached before it must be asked for again.
AWS Certificate Manager: free, trusted TLS certificates for load balancers and other AWS services, renewed automatically.
A file proving a key belongs to a domain, signed by an authority browsers trust. It is what puts the padlock on HTTPS.
A certificate you made yourself. The traffic is encrypted, but nobody trusted vouches for it, so browsers warn.
Decrypting HTTPS at the load balancer, so the servers behind it never handle certificates.
The five addresses AWS keeps in every subnet: the first four and the last. A /24 has 256 addresses but only 251 you can use.
The number after the slash in a CIDR range, like the 24 in /24. It is how many bits are fixed; the rest decide how many addresses the range holds.
One of the four numbers in an IPv4 address, from 0 to 255. Each is 8 bits, so an address is 32 bits.
A private connection between two VPCs. It only works if their address ranges don't overlap.
The route for the VPC's own range, present in every route table and impossible to remove. It lets everything in a VPC reach everything else.
The route table a VPC starts with. Any subnet not given its own table uses it, so it is safest left with only the local route.
The rule for choosing between routes: when several match a packet, the one with the biggest number after the slash wins.
A private path from your VPC to an AWS service such as S3 or Secrets Manager, so the traffic never goes over the internet.
A free VPC endpoint for S3 or DynamoDB. It works by adding a route for the service's prefix list to your route tables.
A VPC endpoint for most other AWS services. It puts a network interface with a private address in your subnet, and bills by the hour.
A named list of address ranges, with an ID starting pl-. AWS keeps one per service, such as S3, and gateway endpoint routes point at it.
How security is split: AWS secures the buildings, hardware and its own services; you secure what you put in them, such as access, network rules, patches and data.
Sends you an alert when spending crosses, or is forecast to cross, a limit you set. It warns; it never stops anything.
An AWS service that isn't tied to one region, such as IAM. The console's region selector shows Global on its pages.
A firewall that remembers each allowed connection and lets its replies back automatically. Security groups are stateful.
A stateless firewall on a whole subnet, with numbered allow and deny rules. Replies need their own rule. Usually left at the default.
The random high-numbered port a client uses for one connection, where the reply comes back. Usually somewhere in 1024 to 65535.
What a load balancer returns when it couldn't get an answer from a server in time. Behind an AWS load balancer, often a security group dropping traffic.
A code like use1-az2 that names the same availability zone in every AWS account. Zone names like us-east-1a can point at different zones in different accounts.
Where AWS reports problems with its own services, by region and zone. Worth checking early in an incident.
